dlab-stress.title: Stress Patterns
dlab-stress.blurb: The DLAB opens with sound: four made-up words, and you pick the one stressed differently. Learn what stress sounds like, the four ranked rules that decide it in the test language, then the odd-one-out format the real test uses.

units.title: Hearing stress and the ending rules
units.objective: Hear which syllable is stressed, and place the stress from the end of a word: last, second-to-last or third-to-last.

steps: Every word of two or more syllables has one syllable that stands out. That syllable is stressed: it is louder, a little longer and usually higher in pitch than the others.
English shows it clearly: baNAna, PHOtograph, phoTOgraphy. The letters barely change, but the stress moves, and you hear it straight away.
On the DLAB you hear made-up words, so meaning can't help you. Listen for the loudest, longest beat. Tapping the beats on the desk with one hard tap for the strongest syllable helps.
In this course the test language also has stress RULES, so you can check your ear in writing. Count syllables from the END of the word, never from the front.

Ending rule: if the word ends in a consonant, the last syllable is stressed. If it ends in a vowel, look at the second-to-last syllable: if that syllable ends in a consonant (it is closed, like 'ral' or 'mon'), stress it.
Default: if the word ends in a vowel and the second-to-last syllable also ends in a vowel, stress the third-to-last syllable.
A closed syllable anywhere else in the word does nothing. Only the last two syllables decide.
teach.formula: Last letter a consonant: stress the last · Else second-to-last closed: stress it · Else: third-to-last

worked.stem: Which syllable takes the main stress in ko-mal-fe-ri-to?
steps: Look at the last letter: to ends in o, a vowel, so the last syllable is not stressed.
Look at the second-to-last syllable: ri ends in i, a vowel. It is open, so rule 3 does not apply.
So the default applies: stress the third-to-last syllable, fe.
mal is closed, but it isn't one of the last two syllables, so it is a trap and changes nothing.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Put your finger on the very last letter of the word.
Is it a consonant (not a, e, i, o, u)? Then the last syllable is stressed. Stop.
If not, move your finger to the end of the second-to-last syllable. Is that letter a consonant? Then that syllable is stressed. Stop.
If not, count back three syllables from the end. That one is stressed.
Ignore everything else in the word: only these checks count.

Second-to-last closed?
Third-to-last

reteach.intro: No problem. Let's read the word backwards, one syllable at a time.
steps: Write the syllables in reverse order: for ko-mal-fe-ri-to that is to, ri, fe, mal, ko.
First item in your list (the last syllable): does it end in a consonant? If yes, it's stressed.
Second item (second-to-last): does it end in a consonant? If yes, it's stressed.
Otherwise, the third item is stressed.
You never need to look past the third item.

units.title: Doubled vowels and the order of the rules
units.objective: Apply the four stress rules in their ranked order, with a doubled vowel beating every ending rule.

steps: Rule 1 sits above all the others: a syllable with a doubled vowel (aa, ee, ii, oo, uu) always takes the stress, wherever it is in the word.
In speech a doubled vowel is a long vowel: you hear it held, like the 'oo' in 'balloon'. Long syllables pull the stress toward them.
So the first thing you check is NOT the end of the word. Scan the whole word for a doubled vowel first. Only if there is none do you move on to the ending rules.
The test likes words where two rules seem to apply: a doubled vowel in the first syllable AND a consonant at the end. The doubled vowel wins.
Work every word with the same four checks, in the same order, and you can't be trapped.
teach.formula: 1 Doubled vowel · 2 Final consonant · 3 Closed second-to-last · 4 Third-to-last

worked.stem: Which syllable takes the main stress in dee-ra-mon-pi-sal?
steps: Check 1: scan for a doubled vowel. dee has 'ee'. Found one.
Rule 1 beats everything, so dee is stressed, even though the word ends in a consonant (sal) and rule 2 would otherwise pick the last syllable.
No other check is needed.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Think of the rules as a ladder. You always start at the top step.
Top step: is there a doubled vowel anywhere? If yes, that syllable is stressed and you are done.
Second step: does the word end in a consonant? If yes, the last syllable.
Third step: does the second-to-last syllable end in a consonant? If yes, that one.
Bottom step: the third-to-last syllable.
Never skip a step, and never go back up once you've stopped.

units.title: Odd one out: the real test format
units.objective: Find the one word of four whose stress falls on a different syllable, first in writing, then by ear.

steps: On the real DLAB you hear four made-up words, each played once, and pick the one whose stress pattern is different. All four have the same number of syllables, and three are stressed on the same one.
In writing, work out each word's stressed syllable with the four checks, then count it from the FRONT (1st, 2nd, 3rd…). Three numbers match; the odd one is the answer.

The traps: the three matching words reach their stress by DIFFERENT rules (one by a doubled vowel, one by a closed second-to-last syllable…), and the odd word is stressed just one syllable away. Check every word fully; never assume.
By ear: as each word plays, tap the beats and mark the strong one on your fingers: thumb for the 1st syllable, first finger for the 2nd, and so on. Compare fingers at the end.
When you're ready, turn on Listening mode in Practice tests (Stress Patterns): the same items are spoken, with the answers read as A to D. In the full mock each item plays only once, as on the test.
teach.formula: Find each word's stressed syllable · Count it from the front · The number that differs is the answer

worked.stem: Which is stressed differently? ka-lo-mun-te, ri-saa-po-le, ve-ni-tal-ko, bo-da-res-mu
steps: ka-lo-mun-te: no doubled vowel, ends in a vowel, mun (second-to-last) is closed, so mun: the 3rd syllable.
ri-saa-po-le: saa has a doubled vowel, so saa: the 2nd syllable.
ve-ni-tal-ko: tal is closed and second-to-last, so tal: the 3rd syllable.
bo-da-res-mu: res is closed and second-to-last, so res: the 3rd syllable.
Three are stressed on the 3rd syllable; ri-saa-po-le is the odd one out.

dlab-nounadj.title: Nouns and Adjectives
dlab-nounadj.blurb: Your first set of grammar rules in the made-up language: where the adjective goes, which vowel it takes, and how plurals and number words change both words. Learn to apply every rule to every word, every time.

units.title: Grammar words you'll need
units.objective: Spot the noun, adjective, verb, subject, object, owner, number, tense, negative and question in any English sentence.

steps: Every DLAB rule is written in grammar words: 'the adjective follows the noun', 'the object takes -na', 'the owner comes after the thing owned'. If those words are fuzzy, the rules are too. Five minutes here saves marks in every section.
A NOUN names a person, animal or thing: man, dog, book. An ADJECTIVE describes a noun: big, black, old. A NUMBER WORD counts it: two, three, four. PLURAL means more than one: dogs.
A VERB is the action: see, chase, find. Its TENSE says when: present (sees), past (saw), future (will see).

The SUBJECT does the action. The OBJECT has the action done to it. In 'The dog chases the cat', the dog is the subject and the cat is the object. Swap them and the meaning flips: 'The cat chases the dog'.
A PRONOUN stands in for a noun: I, you, he, we, they. Words like my, your, his, our, their show an OWNER. In 'the man's dog', the man is the owner and the dog is the thing owned.
A NEGATIVE says something does not happen (does not see). A QUESTION asks (Does the dog see the cat?). The subject, object and tense stay the same; only the frame around them changes.
teach.formula: Who does it = subject · Who it's done to = object · When = tense · Whose = owner

worked.stem: "Will the old man's dogs not find the red ball?" Name each part.
steps: Verb: find. 'Will' makes it future tense.
'not' makes it negative, and the word order makes it a question.
Who does the finding? The dogs: they are the subject (plural).
Whose dogs? The old man's: the man is the owner, and old describes him.
What is found? The ball: it is the object, and red describes it.
worked.answer: Subject: dogs (owner: old man) · Verb: find, future, negative question · Object: red ball

Look for 's or my/your/his/our/their: that's an owner.

practice.explain: 'Did … see' is the past tense turned into a question. Questions and negatives keep their tense.

Is there a number word (two, three, four) or more than one? That's plural.

units.title: Adjective position and vowel
units.objective: Place the adjective after its noun and give it the last vowel of the noun's root.

steps: On the DLAB you are given rules and a few words, then asked to build or recognize new phrases at once. You don't memorize a language: you apply rules exactly, like following a checklist.
Rule: the adjective comes AFTER the noun. English says 'big dog'; this language says 'dog big'.
Adjectives are listed as stems that end in a consonant: big- (big), blak- (black). The stem never appears on its own.
Rule: the adjective takes the LAST vowel of its noun's root. dogo (dog) ends in o, so big = bigo: dogo bigo. kate (cat) ends in e, so dogo's adjective and kate's adjective differ: kate more.
The trap answers use the noun's FIRST vowel (dogo, a: biga), the wrong position (bigo dogo), or the bare stem (big). Check position and vowel on every adjective.
Plural adds -s to the noun and to every adjective: dogos bigos. There is no word for 'the' or 'a'.

On the real test you see only the English; the four answers are SPOKEN ("A … B … C … D …"), once. Build the right phrase in your head BEFORE the answers play, then listen for it. Practice that with Listening mode in Practice tests.
teach.formula: Noun first · Adjective = stem + noun's LAST vowel · Plural: -s on both

worked.stem: Words: horse = horsu, black = blak-. How do you say "the black horses"?
steps: Noun first: horsu. It's plural, so horsus.
The root horsu ends in u, so black = blak + u = blaku.
The adjective is plural too: blakus.
Adjective after the noun: horsus blakus.

practice.passage:
Rules for this section:
1. An adjective comes after the noun it describes.
2. An adjective is a stem ending in a consonant (blak- = black). It takes the last vowel of its noun's root: dogo (dog) gives dogo blako.
3. Plural: add -s to the noun and to each of its adjectives.
4. After a number word (tuo = two, thri = three, fora = four), the number comes first and neither the noun nor its adjectives take -s.
5. With two adjectives, both follow the noun in the REVERSE of the English order.
6. There is no word for "the" or "a".

steps: Number words come FIRST: tuo (two), thri (three), fora (four).

steps: The DLAB adds rules section by section, and the old rules never switch off. Here every noun and adjective rule still applies.

steps: English puts the owner first: the man's dog. This language puts it AFTER: dogo manuve.

dlab-verbs.title: Verbs, Subjects and Objects
dlab-verbs.blurb: Whole sentences: subject, object, then the verb last. Mark the object with -na, pick the tense ending, add -en when the subject is plural and nu- for not. The noun and adjective rules still apply to every noun.

units.title: Subject, object, verb, and the -na marker
units.objective: Put the verb last, mark the object noun with -na after all its other endings, and use the pronouns.

steps: Word order is subject, then object, then verb. The verb is ALWAYS the last word.
The object (the one the action is done to) is marked: its noun takes -na. It goes after every other ending: dogos + na = dogosna (the dogs, as object).
Only the noun takes -na. Its adjectives stay as they were: dogosna bigos. A trap answer puts -na on the adjective at the end of the phrase.
The adjective's vowel still comes from the noun's root, not from -na: katena blake (cat, black), not katena blaka.
Pronouns: mi (I), ti (you), si (he or she), mis (we), sis (they). As objects they take -na: mina (me), tina (you), sina (him), misna (us), sisna (them).
Verbs are stems plus a tense ending. Present is -ar: luk- (see) becomes lukar.

worked.stem: Words: dog = dogo, cat = kate, black = blak-, see = luk-. How do you say "The dog sees the black cat"?
steps: Subject first: dogo.
Object next, with -na on the noun: katena. Its adjective takes e from kate: blake.
Verb last, present: lukar.
Result: dogo katena blake lukar.

units.title: Tense, plural subjects and nu-
units.objective: Build the verb: nu- for not, the stem, the tense ending, then -en if the subject is plural.

steps: Tense endings: -ar (present), -ir (past), -ul (future). lukar = sees, lukir = saw, lukul = will see.
If the SUBJECT is plural, add -en after the tense ending: lukiren = (they) saw.

Plural subject means three things: a noun with -s, a noun after a number word (no -s, but still plural), or the pronouns mis (we) and sis (they). The number-word case is the classic trap: tuo boyi ... still needs -en.
Only the subject counts. A plural OBJECT never adds -en.
Not = nu- on the front of the verb: nulukiren = (they) did not see.
So a verb is built in a fixed order: nu-, stem, tense, -en. Distractors put -en before the tense, nu at the end, or -en for a plural object.
teach.formula: (nu-) + stem + -ar / -ir / -ul + (-en if the subject is plural)

dlab-rules.title: Comprehensive Rules
dlab-rules.blurb: Every rule at once: owners, possessive endings, number words, the object marker, tense, plural subjects, negatives and the new question word ka. Learn one routine for building long sentences and one for reading them back.

units.title: Building long sentences in order
units.objective: Build any sentence with one routine: ka, subject phrase, object phrase with -na, verb, then check endings.

steps: The final audio section of the DLAB mixes every rule you've learned, in longer phrases, with little time per item. The way through is a fixed routine.
New rule: a yes/no question starts with ka. Nothing else changes: same word order, same endings, verb still last.
Routine: 1) ka if it's a yes/no question. 2) The subject phrase. 3) The object phrase. 4) The verb.
Each phrase is built the same way: number word, noun with its endings, its adjectives (reversed if two), then any owner with -ve and the owner's adjectives.
Endings on one noun always stack: plural -s, then my/your/his/our/their, then -ve (owner), then -na (object).
The verb: nu- if negative, stem, tense, then -en if the SUBJECT is plural.
Long items usually hide one error in a long correct-looking option. Check one rule at a time across all four options, and cross options out as soon as one rule fails.
teach.formula: ka · Subject phrase · Object phrase + -na · nu- + verb + tense + (-en)

Rules for this section:

2. An adjective is a stem ending in a consonant (blak- = black). It takes the last vowel of its noun's root: dogo (dog) gives dogo blako.
3. Plural: add -s to the noun and to each of its adjectives.
4. After a number word (tuo = two, thri = three, fora = four), the number comes first and neither the noun nor its adjectives take -s.
5. With two adjectives, both follow the noun in the REVERSE of the English order.
6. There is no word for "the" or "a".
7. my, your, his, our, their are endings on the noun: -mi, -ti, -si, -mis, -sis.
8. The owner comes AFTER the thing owned and takes the ending -ve: dogo manuve = the man's dog.
9. The thing owned keeps its adjectives right after it; the owner's adjectives follow the owner.
10. Endings go on in this order: plural -s, then my/your/his/our/their, then -ve.
11. An adjective's vowel comes from its own noun's root, never from an ending.

units.title: Reading sentences back to English
units.objective: Decode a long sentence by peeling endings: find ka, the verb, the -na word and the -ve word, then read each phrase.

steps: On a 'What does it mean?' item, don't translate left to right. Find the landmarks first.
Landmark 1: ka at the start means it's a question.
Landmark 2: the last word is the verb. Read it from both ends: nu- (not), the stem, the tense (-ar, -ir, -ul), and -en (the subject is plural).

11. An adjective's vowel comes from its own noun's root, never from an ending.
